newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Twelve KAL crash survivors airlifted to S.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Twelve KAL crash survivors airlifted to S.Korea.

text.p: Twelve people who survived the crash of a Korean Air Lines (KAL) Boeing 747 on the Pacific island of Guam were airlifted to South Korea on Saturday.

Covered in bandages and white sheets, the survivors were lowered on stretchers from a U.S. C-9 Nightingale medical evacuation plane. Ambulances with police escorts took them four burns units and hospitals in town.

The same plane had brought back eight other survivors a day earlier. Doctors said none of them were in life-threatening condition, but KAL officials said three Korean nationals who remained on the island were critical.
"I am happy to return alive, but I am sorry for those who died," Kim Min-suk, 29, who suffered minor burns, told Korean media before leaving Guam.
Kim's wife, who also survived, was among those left behind after suffering burns on about 60 percent of her body.

Just 27 of the 254 people on board survived when the jumbo jet ploughed into a hilltop while attempting to land on the Pacific island in heavy rain. Five others were alive when pulled from the smouldering wreckage, but died later in hospital.
Family members anxiously waiting for the survivors at the hospital wailed when they saw loved ones arriving with noticeable cuts and burns.
Two of the survivors who arrived on Saturday had suffered burns over 40 percent of their bodies and were admitted to intensive care units at burns centres.
Investigators have recovered half of the bodies from the wreckage scattered over hilly jungle terrain in sight of the runway, but rescuers have given up hope of finding any more survivors.
A Korean doctor said on Friday that survivors of the crash had shown great mental strength amid the anguish felt for their dead loved ones.
"All of those we've treated are incredibly strong mentally, especially considering their experience and their loss," said Dr Moon G. Yoon of Guam Memorial Hospital.
Nine Taiwanese monks and nuns flew to Guam on Friday and held a Buddhist memorial service for a number of the victims.
The mourners wailed, chanted and burned incense during the service at a makeshift altar near the crash site, with the aircraft's tailplane visible in the background.
KAL officials in Seoul said a mourning site for bereaved families would be set up at a gymnasium close to the airport on Saturday.
U.S. safety investigators said it was too early to determine what caused the crash, but that the jet did not suffer any engine or structural failure before crashing.
The investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) also said the crew were apparently not aware of any problem as the aircraft approached the airport.
In Seoul, KAL officials cautioned against giving credence to reports in U.S. media that the accident had been caused by pilot error.

"We are not yet ruling out the possibility of a sudden change in altitude caused by torrential rains, the breakdown of the glide slope or other elements which, combined, could have caused the accident," KAL said.
